By Dirichlet’s theorem, choose a prime \(q\equiv1\pmod 4\) such that \(q>\max\{y,x+1\}\). Since \(-1\) is a quadratic residue modulo \(q\), choose \(s\) with \(s^2\equiv-1\pmod q\). As \(q\nmid y\), choose \(a\not\equiv0\pmod q\) satisfying \(ay\equiv s\pmod q\).

For every positive integer \(n\equiv a\pmod q\), we then have
\[
q\mid (ny)^2+1,
\]
so the hypothesis gives
\[
x^{\varphi(n)}\equiv1\pmod q.
\]
Because \(q>x\), let \(d=\operatorname{ord}_q(x)\). Thus \(d\mid\varphi(n)\) for every such \(n\), and \(d\mid q-1\).

Suppose \(d>2\). Since \(\gcd(d,q)=1\), the Chinese remainder theorem gives a reduced residue class \(c\pmod{qd}\) satisfying
\[
c\equiv a\pmod q,\qquad c\equiv-1\pmod d.
\]
By Dirichlet’s theorem, this class contains a prime \(r\). Taking \(n=r\), the preceding congruence implies
\[
d\mid\varphi(r)=r-1.
\]
But \(r\equiv-1\pmod d\), so \(r-1\equiv-2\pmod d\), forcing \(d\mid2\), a contradiction. Hence \(d\le2\), and therefore
\[
x^2\equiv1\pmod q.
\]
Thus \(q\mid(x-1)(x+1)\). Since \(1\le x<q-1\), this is possible only when \(x-1=0\). Consequently, \(x=1\).

Assume for contradiction that x>1. Taking n=2, since φ(2)=1, gives

4y²+1 | x-1.

Choose a prime q dividing 4y²+1. Then (2y)² ≡ -1 (mod q), so q≡1 (mod 4), hence q≥5, and q∤y. Also q|x-1. Put c=v_q(x-1), which is finite.

We prove that for every K≥1 there exists a positive integer n such that

q^K | n²y²+1  and  q∤φ(n).

Let f(T)=y²T²+1. We have f(2)≡0 (mod q), while f'(2)=4y² is nonzero modulo q. Thus Hensel lifting gives a residue r_K modulo q^K such that

r_K≡2 (mod q),   f(r_K)≡0 (mod q^K).

Set g=(q-1)². Since v_q(g-1)=1, LTE gives

v_q(g^{q^j}-1)=j+1.

Consequently g has order q^{K-1} modulo q^K and generates the group of residues congruent to 1 modulo q. Because r_K(q+2)^{-1}≡1 (mod q), there is some t≥0 such that

(q+2)g^t≡r_K (mod q^K).

Define n=(q+2)(q-1)^{2t}. Then n≡r_K (mod q^K), so q^K|n²y²+1.

Every prime divisor ℓ of n divides either q-1 or q+2. Hence ℓ≠q and ℓ≢1 (mod q): indeed, the only integer in [2,q+2] congruent to 1 modulo q is q+1, which is even and greater than 2, so is not prime. From the formula for φ(n), it follows that q∤φ(n).

Now choose K>c and take the corresponding n. The hypothesis yields

q^K | n²y²+1 | x^{φ(n)}-1.

On the other hand, since q is odd, q|x-1, and q∤φ(n), LTE gives

v_q(x^{φ(n)}-1)=v_q(x-1)+v_q(φ(n))=c<K,

a contradiction. Therefore x>1 is impossible. Since x is a positive integer, x=1.

Assume the stated divisibility holds for every positive integer n.

Fix any prime q≡1 (mod 4) with q∤y. Since −1 is a quadratic residue modulo q, choose a∈{1,…,q−1} such that (ay)^2≡−1 (mod q). Taking n=a shows q∣x^{φ(a)}−1, so q∤x. Let r=ord_q(x); then r∣q−1.

We claim r≤2. Otherwise r>2. Since gcd(q,r)=1, the Chinese remainder theorem gives a reduced residue class b modulo qr satisfying
b≡a (mod q),  b≡−1 (mod r).
By Dirichlet's theorem on primes in arithmetic progressions, choose a prime p≡b (mod qr). Then q∣(py)^2+1, so the hypothesis with n=p gives
q∣x^{φ(p)}−1=x^{p−1}−1.
Hence r∣p−1. But p≡−1 (mod r), so r∣2, contradicting r>2. Thus r≤2, and consequently q∣x^2−1.

There are infinitely many primes q≡1 (mod 4), and only finitely many divide y. Therefore infinitely many primes divide x^2−1. This is possible only if x^2−1=0. Since x is positive, x=1.

problem.theorem:
Let \( x \) and \( y \) be positive integers. If for each positive integer \( n \) we have that

\[
(n y)^{2}+1 \mid x^{\varphi(n)}-1
\]

prove that \( x=1 \).
